questions.questionText: What is the function of a firewall in a network?

options.text: To boost the wireless signal throughout a building
To filter network traffic based on rules, allowing or blocking connections
To assign IP addresses to network hosts
To increase the speed of internet connections

explanation.correct: A firewall controls inbound and outbound network traffic based on configured security rules, blocking unauthorised access while allowing legitimate traffic.
explanation.incorrect: Wireless boosting = WAP/repeater. IP assignment = DHCP. Speed increase = QoS/bandwidth upgrade.
explanation.examTip: Stateless firewall = inspects individual packets only. Stateful = tracks connection state. Next-gen firewall (NGFW) = also inspects application layer.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?

options.text: IDS blocks threats; IPS only detects them
IDS detects and alerts on threats; IPS detects and actively blocks them inline
IPS operates at Layer 7; IDS operates at Layer 3
IDS is hardware only; IPS is software only

explanation.correct: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors and alerts. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) is deployed inline and can actively block malicious traffic in real time.
explanation.incorrect: IDS = passive detection. IPS = active blocking. Both can operate at multiple OSI layers. Both can be hardware or software.
explanation.examTip: IDS = out-of-band (tap/SPAN port), can't block. IPS = inline, can block. IPS must be inline to intercept traffic.

questions.questionText: What is a DMZ in network security?

options.text: A VLAN used exclusively for management traffic
A network segment that hosts public-facing services, isolated from the internal network
A wireless network zone for guest users
A VPN tunnel between two sites

explanation.correct: A DMZ (Demilitarised Zone) is a perimeter network segment that hosts public-facing servers (web, email, DNS), positioned between the internet and the internal network with firewalls on both sides.
explanation.incorrect: Management VLAN is separate. Guest wireless is a different concept. VPNs are encrypted tunnels.
explanation.examTip: DMZ architecture: Internet â†’ Firewall â†’ DMZ (public servers) â†’ Firewall â†’ Internal network. Even if DMZ is compromised, internal network is protected.

questions.questionText: Which attack overwhelms a target with traffic from a single source to make it unavailable?

options.text: DDoS
DoS
Man-in-the-middle
ARP poisoning

explanation.correct: A DoS (Denial of Service) attack originates from a single source and floods a target with traffic or requests to exhaust its resources and make it unavailable.
explanation.incorrect: DDoS = multiple sources (distributed). MitM = intercepts communications. ARP poisoning = redirects Layer 2 traffic.
explanation.examTip: DoS = single source. DDoS = multiple sources (botnet). DDoS is harder to mitigate because you can't just block one IP.

questions.scenarioText: A network admin discovers that a host on the LAN is sending gratuitous ARP replies claiming to be the default gateway, redirecting all traffic through itself.
questions.questionText: What type of attack is occurring and what switch feature can prevent it?

options.text: VLAN hopping; prevent with BPDU Guard
ARP poisoning; prevent with Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
DHCP spoofing; prevent with DHCP Snooping
MAC flooding; prevent with port security

explanation.correct: ARP poisoning sends fake ARP replies to poison the ARP caches of other hosts, redirecting traffic through the attacker (MitM). Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table.
explanation.incorrect: VLAN hopping exploits trunk negotiation. DHCP spoofing provides fake IP configs. MAC flooding fills the CAM table forcing hub-like behaviour.
explanation.examTip: DAI requires DHCP Snooping to be enabled first â€” it uses the DHCP snooping binding table to validate ARP replies.

questions.questionText: What does 802.1X provide in a network environment?

options.text: Link aggregation across multiple switch ports
Port-based network access control requiring authentication before granting LAN access
VLAN assignment based on interface speed
Encryption of traffic between switches

explanation.correct: 802.1X is an IEEE standard for port-based NAC. Devices must authenticate (via RADIUS) before the switch grants access to the network, blocking unauthenticated devices.
explanation.incorrect: Link aggregation = LACP (802.3ad). VLAN by speed is not a standard. Traffic encryption = MACsec (802.1AE).
explanation.examTip: 802.1X roles: Supplicant (device), Authenticator (switch/AP), Authentication Server (RADIUS). EAP is the authentication protocol used.

questions.questionText: Which VPN protocol encapsulates the entire original IP packet and adds a new header, commonly used for site-to-site VPNs?

options.text: IPSec Transport mode
IPSec Tunnel mode
SSL/TLS VPN
PPTP

explanation.correct: IPSec Tunnel mode encapsulates the entire original IP packet (header + payload) and adds a new outer IP header, used for site-to-site VPNs between gateways.
explanation.incorrect: Transport mode encrypts only the payload, used for host-to-host. SSL/TLS VPN uses web browser or lightweight client. PPTP is legacy and insecure.
explanation.examTip: Tunnel mode = site-to-site (whole packet encrypted). Transport mode = host-to-host (payload only). Always use Tunnel mode for site-to-site VPNs.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes network security concepts.

statements.text: A stateful firewall tracks the state of active connections and uses this context in filtering decisions.
WPA2-Enterprise uses a pre-shared key for authentication.
DHCP Snooping prevents rogue DHCP servers from providing false IP configuration to clients.
Port security can prevent MAC flooding attacks by limiting the number of MAC addresses per port.

explanation.correct: Stateful firewalls track connections. DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP. Port security limits MACs per port preventing flooding. WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS (not PSK â€” that's WPA2-Personal).
explanation.incorrect: WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X authentication with individual credentials, not a shared key.
explanation.examTip: WPA2-Personal = PSK (pre-shared key). WPA2-Enterprise = 802.1X (individual credentials via RADIUS).

questions.questionText: Which attack exploits double-tagging of 802.1Q frames to send traffic from one VLAN to another without routing?

options.text: ARP poisoning
MAC flooding
VLAN hopping
STP manipulation

explanation.correct: VLAN hopping via double-tagging adds two 802.1Q tags to a frame. The first switch strips the outer tag, and the inner tag tricks the second switch into delivering the frame to the target VLAN.
explanation.incorrect: ARP poisoning targets Layer 2 ARP tables. MAC flooding fills the CAM table. STP manipulation attacks the spanning tree topology.
explanation.examTip: Prevent VLAN hopping: set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN ID, explicitly tag native VLAN traffic, and don't use VLAN 1 as native VLAN.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a proxy server?

options.text: To assign IP addresses to network clients
To act as an intermediary between clients and servers, providing content filtering, caching, and anonymity
To encrypt traffic between two VPN endpoints
To provide redundancy for critical network services

explanation.correct: A proxy server intercepts client requests, providing content filtering (block malicious sites), caching (improve performance), and hiding client IPs (anonymity/privacy).
explanation.incorrect: IP assignment = DHCP. VPN encryption = VPN gateway. Redundancy = clustering/failover.
explanation.examTip: Forward proxy = client â†’ proxy â†’ internet (client anonymity). Reverse proxy = internet â†’ proxy â†’ servers (server protection, load balancing).

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of port security on a switch?

options.text: To block all traffic on a port until it is manually enabled
To limit the number of MAC addresses allowed on a port and take action on violations
To encrypt traffic between the switch and connected devices
To prevent STP topology changes

explanation.correct: Port security restricts the number of MAC addresses allowed per switch port, preventing MAC flooding attacks and unauthorised devices from connecting.
explanation.incorrect: Admin shutdown = different from port security. Switch doesn't encrypt traffic. BPDU Guard/Root Guard prevent STP attacks.
explanation.examTip: Port security violation modes: protect (drop frames, no alert), restrict (drop + alert), shutdown (err-disable port). Use sticky MAC to auto-learn allowed MACs.

questions.questionText: Which attack involves an attacker sending a large volume of SYN packets without completing the TCP three-way handshake?

options.text: Smurf attack
SYN flood
Ping of Death
Teardrop attack

explanation.correct: A SYN flood sends massive numbers of TCP SYN packets without completing the handshake, filling the server's connection queue (half-open connections) and preventing legitimate connections.
explanation.incorrect: Smurf = ICMP amplification using broadcast. Ping of Death = oversized ping packets. Teardrop = malformed fragmented packets.
explanation.examTip: SYN flood defense: SYN cookies (server doesn't allocate resources until handshake complete), rate limiting, firewall connection limits.

questions.questionText: What is a honeypot in the context of network security?

options.text: A device that speeds up network performance by caching data
A decoy system designed to attract and detect attackers
A type of VPN used for remote access
A network device that filters spam emails

explanation.correct: A honeypot is a decoy system that mimics a real target to attract attackers, allowing security teams to observe attack techniques and gather threat intelligence without risk to production systems.
explanation.incorrect: Caching = proxy/CDN. VPN = encrypted tunnel. Email filtering = spam filter/mail gateway.
explanation.examTip: Honeypot = decoy server. Honeynet = network of honeypots. Any interaction with a honeypot is suspicious by definition.

questions.questionText: Which protocol provides encrypted management access to network devices, replacing Telnet?

options.text: SNMP
Telnet
SSH
HTTP

explanation.correct: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted terminal access to network devices, replacing Telnet which transmits all data including passwords in cleartext.
explanation.incorrect: SNMP = network management protocol. Telnet = insecure cleartext. HTTP = unencrypted web.
explanation.examTip: Always use SSH v2 (never v1 or Telnet). SSH uses TCP port 22. Also use for secure file transfer (SFTP/SCP).

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes network security concepts.

statements.text: A VLAN on its own provides strong security isolation equivalent to a physical firewall.
Disabling unused switch ports reduces the attack surface of a network.
MAC address filtering alone provides strong wireless security.
Changing the default SNMP community string 'public' is an important hardening step.

explanation.correct: VLANs provide logical separation but are vulnerable to VLAN hopping attacks. Disabling unused ports prevents physical access. Default SNMP community strings must be changed. MAC filtering is easily bypassed by MAC spoofing.
explanation.incorrect: VLANs and MAC filtering alone are insufficient security controls.
explanation.examTip: Network hardening checklist: disable unused ports, change default credentials, use SNMPv3, enable port security, use 802.1X, segment with firewalls + VLANs.

questions.scenarioText: A security admin wants to prevent users from connecting unauthorised devices (like personal laptops) to the corporate network.
questions.questionText: Which technology is MOST effective at enforcing this policy?

options.text: MAC address filtering on the switches
802.1X port-based Network Access Control
Disabling DHCP
Changing the SSID broadcast setting

explanation.correct: 802.1X requires devices to authenticate (via certificates or credentials) before the switch grants network access. Unauthorised devices without valid credentials are blocked at the port level.
explanation.incorrect: MAC filtering is easily bypassed by MAC spoofing. Disabling DHCP still allows static IP assignment. SSID settings are wireless-only and don't prevent wired connections.
explanation.examTip: 802.1X with certificate-based authentication (EAP-TLS) is the strongest NAC option â€” only domain-joined devices with valid certs can connect.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a content filter in a network?

options.text: To increase the speed of internet access
To inspect and block access to websites or content based on categories or keywords
To encrypt web traffic between users and websites
To cache web content to reduce bandwidth usage

explanation.correct: Content filters inspect web traffic and block access to prohibited categories (adult content, gambling, malware sites) based on policies â€” commonly deployed as a web proxy or DNS filtering service.
explanation.incorrect: Speed acceleration = QoS/CDN. Encryption = TLS/VPN. Caching = web proxy (caching function specifically).
explanation.examTip: Content filtering can be URL-based, DNS-based (e.g., Cisco Umbrella), or deep packet inspection. Also helps block malware download sites.

questions.questionText: What does AAA stand for in network security?

options.text: Authentication, Authorisation, Accounting
Access, Administration, Auditing
Availability, Accuracy, Accountability
Authorisation, Accessibility, Archiving

explanation.correct: AAA = Authentication (verify identity), Authorisation (determine access rights), Accounting (log what was done). Implemented by RADIUS or TACACS+ servers.
explanation.incorrect: The other options are not the correct AAA definition.
explanation.examTip: RADIUS = AAA for network access (UDP 1812/1813). TACACS+ = AAA for device management (TCP 49, Cisco). Both provide centralised authentication.
